strengths: Well-motivated systematic probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) that clearly isolates and demonstrates a specific weakness of LLM world models: degradation in long-horizon procedural alignment despite strong short-horizon prediction.

The proposed R-WoM framework is a clean, practically motivated combination of reasoning-based RAG (query rewriting + LLM reranking), single-pass LongCoT rollout (vs. costly iterative rollout), and listwise (relative) reward estimation instead of absolute scoring.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two realistic and challenging benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena) and three different backbone LLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3.7-Sonnet), showing consistent gains over Vanilla, RAG, and WoM baselines.

Thoughtful ablations addressing RQ2 (oracle vs retrieved vs no grounding) and RQ3 (performance vs imagination horizon), which directly support the paper's central claim that grounding helps stabilize long-horizon rollouts.

Detailed appendix with prompts, tutorial sources, domain-level breakdowns, retrieval ablations (query rewriting/reranking), and a careful cost/efficiency analysis comparing to iterative rollout (WebDreamer), improving transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The probing tasks use relatively small sample sizes (100, 40, and 98 examples respectively split across two benchmarks and three models), limiting the statistical robustness of the preliminary analysis that motivates the whole paper.

The full-procedure planning alignment task is judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet, which is also one of the models being evaluated on this task, raising concerns about self-evaluation bias in the probing results.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: retrieval-augmented grounding, LLM reranking, and listwise (relative) reward/ranking are all well-established ideas individually; the main contribution is their combination for world-model rollouts rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

End-to-end absolute success rates remain modest (roughly 26-41% on OSWorld and 22-35% on WebArena even with R-WoM), and some baseline comparisons (e.g., Claude-3.5 Vanilla vs RAG on OSWorld) have overlapping error bars, making certain individual improvements less convincing.

Experiments are restricted to curated task subsets where tutorials are available and where the authors themselves manually annotated 'oracle' reference chunks, which were also used to build/evaluate retrieval and full-procedure alignment; this manual curation could introduce selection bias and limits generalizability to the full benchmarks or tutorial-scarce domains (acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically explored).

The WoM baseline is the authors' own reimplementation of WebDreamer using LongCoT rather than the original iterative approach, and other recent world-model baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., WKM, WebEvolver) are not included in the end-to-end comparison, weakening the completeness of the baseline comparison.

No formal ablation isolating the individual contribution of listwise reward estimation versus absolute reward within the R-WoM framework itself (the comparison is only indirect via WoM vs R-WoM, which differs in grounding as well).

strengths: The paper conducts a clear systematic probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) that motivates the proposed method with reasonably interpretable findings about where LLM world models fail.

The R-WoM framework (query rewriting + LLM reranking for retrieval, LongCoT single-pass rollout, listwise reward ranking) is well described with detailed prompts and algorithmic summary, aiding reproducibility of the pipeline itself.

Reports consistent improvements over Vanilla/RAG/WoM baselines across three different backbones (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5, Claude-3.7) and two benchmarks, with multiple runs and standard deviations provided.

Includes a reasonably thorough appendix with ablations on imagination horizon, retrieval strategy (query rewriting vs reranking), domain-level breakdowns, and a cost/efficiency comparison against an iterative rollout baseline (WebDreamer-style), showing awareness of practical trade-offs.
The oracle-tutorial comparison (Figure 3) is a sensible analysis to isolate the contribution of retrieval quality versus grounding itself.
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted on small, non-standard subsets of OSWorld (85 tasks) and WebArena (113 tasks) that were specifically selected because tutorials are available/mappable; this introduces selection bias favoring the proposed method and makes reported numbers incomparable to the broader literature on these benchmarks, undermining claims of general effectiveness.

The probing study sample sizes are very small (e.g., 40 samples for full-procedure alignment across two benchmarks combined, 98 for milestone recognition, 100 for next-state identification), which is insufficient to draw robust conclusions about fundamental LLM world-modeling limitations, and only three LLMs are tested.

The core technical contribution is an incremental combination of fairly standard components (query rewriting, LLM-based reranking, long-CoT rollout instead of iterative rollout, listwise instead of pointwise reward) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; no ablation isolates the individual contribution of listwise reward vs. absolute reward, so this claimed design choice is unvalidated in isolation.

Absolute task success rates remain low (roughly 26-41% on OSWorld, 29-35% on WebArena even with R-WoM), raising questions about the practical significance/maturity of the approach despite relative percentage gains being emphasized.

The gap between R-WoM with retrieved tutorials and R-WoM with oracle tutorials is often small (e.g., Claude-3.5 on OSWorld: 25.8% vs 27.0%), suggesting retrieval quality is not the dominant bottleneck and somewhat undercutting the motivation for the elaborate reasoning-based RAG pipeline.

The framework fundamentally depends on availability and manual curation of task-relevant tutorial chunks (one/two chunks manually annotated per task, 30k curated chunks from a fixed list of websites), which is acknowledged as a major limitation but also raises reproducibility and scalability concerns for new domains or tasks without existing documentation.

The WoM baseline is a reimplementation/variant of WebDreamer rather than the original method, and comparisons to other related co-evolving world-model approaches mentioned in related work (WKM, WebEvolver) are entirely absent from experiments, limiting the strength of the empirical positioning.

The LLM-as-judge evaluation used both for full-procedure planning alignment probing and implicitly for other components introduces potential circularity/bias (e.g., Claude-3.7-Sonnet is both an evaluated model and the default judge), which is not addressed via inter-rater or alternative-judge validation.

strengths: Well-motivated systematic probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) that clearly diagnoses a specific weakness of LLM-based world models—degradation over long horizons—providing useful empirical grounding for the proposed method.

The proposed R-WoM framework directly addresses the diagnosed weakness via tutorial-grounded retrieval, with a sensible reasoning-based RAG pipeline (query rewriting + LLM reranking) and a listwise reward estimation scheme that is more efficient than prior iterative rollout approaches.

Comprehensive empirical validation across two realistic and challenging benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena) and three different LLM backbones (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet), showing consistent improvements over Vanilla, RAG, and WoM baselines.

Good set of ablations: oracle vs retrieved tutorial grounding, imagination horizon sweep showing R-WoM mitigates compounding rollout errors, and retrieval component ablations (query rewriting/reranking).

Transparent discussion of computational cost/efficiency trade-offs versus iterative world model baselines (WebDreamer-style), which is a practically relevant consideration often omitted in similar papers.
Detailed appendix with prompts, task construction details, and action space specification supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (standard RAG query rewriting/reranking, listwise ranking inspired by prior work, LongCoT rollout), which limits the novelty of the method itself beyond the grounding idea.

Evaluation subsets are small and selected specifically because tutorials are available (85 OSWorld tasks, 113 WebArena tasks), which could bias results favorably toward the proposed retrieval-grounded approach and limits generalizability claims to tutorial-scarce settings (an acknowledged limitation).
The full-procedure planning alignment probing task relies on only 40 annotated samples, which raises concerns about the statistical robustness of a key motivating finding.
Absolute end-to-end success rates remain fairly low (roughly 26-39% on OSWorld, 28-35% on WebArena), raising questions about the practical maturity of the approach despite relative improvements.

The WoM baseline is a reimplementation (LongCoT variant) rather than the original iterative WebDreamer method, and this modification happens to align with design choices favoring R-WoM, which could affect the fairness of the main comparison.
No comparison to stronger/more recent end-to-end computer-use agent frameworks (e.g., Agent S2, UI-TARS) as baselines; comparisons are limited to ablation-style variants built on the same backbones.
Some reported variances in Table 2 (e.g., ±0.01 for Claude-3.5 on WebArena) appear implausibly small given only three runs, raising minor concerns about reporting consistency.
Limited qualitative/error analysis beyond the single illustrative example in Figure 1; it would strengthen the paper to show more failure case breakdowns of where grounding helps or fails.

strengths: Systematic and well-designed probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) that clearly demonstrates a specific failure mode of LLM world models — degradation over long-horizon planning despite strong short-horizon prediction — providing good motivation for the proposed method.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three backbone models (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet, plus extended results with Claude-4/4.5-Sonnet) and two realistic, challenging benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena), with consistent gains over Vanilla, RAG, and WebDreamer baselines.

Extensive ablations covering retrieval component quality (query rewriting + reranking, recall@k), grounding quality (ungrounded vs retrieved vs oracle tutorials), imagination horizon sensitivity, listwise vs absolute reward design, candidate size, and judge robustness (cross-judge consistency), which strengthens the credibility of the design choices.

Thoughtful engineering for efficiency (adaptive action branching, deduplication, LongCoT single-pass rollout instead of iterative rollouts) with a clear cost-performance tradeoff analysis (token usage, latency, WM trigger reduction) which improves practical applicability.

Addresses a realistic and understudied problem: knowledge scarcity and grounding for world models in complex, realistic computer-use environments (as opposed to text-based or video-only settings), including a tutorial-scarce extension via self-play synthesis.
Detailed appendix with prompts, dataset/tutorial source details, and reproducibility information.
weaknesses: Evaluation subsets are quite small (e.g., 100/40/98 samples for probing tasks; 87/361 OSWorld and 113/301 WebArena tasks for main experiments), and the main experiments are restricted to the subset of tasks with tutorial coverage, which may bias results in favor of R-WoM and limits generalizability claims to the full benchmark distributions.

The core technical contribution is a fairly incremental combination of established techniques (RAG with query rewriting/reranking, LongCoT rollout, listwise reward ranking) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty over prior tutorial-augmented agent works (AgentTrek, TongUI, Learn-by-Interact) and world-model works (WebDreamer, WMA, WebEvolver) is mainly in combining them for inference-time grounding.

Reported relative improvements vary widely across models and benchmarks (5.6%–23.4%) without deeper analysis explaining this variance, making it hard to assess how robust/predictable the method's benefit is.

The full-procedure planning alignment judgment relies on an LLM judge (Claude-3.7-Sonnet by default) checked against only two other judges on a small sample, which may not fully rule out judge bias, especially since the same model family is both policy/world model and (in some cases) evaluator.

No direct comparison against other recent world-model baselines explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., WKM, WebEvolver) despite these being close competitors; only WebDreamer is used as the grounded/ungrounded world-model baseline.

The oracle-tutorial experiments rely on manual, human-curated tutorial annotation, which is not scalable and somewhat limits the practical takeaway about real-world retrieval-only performance ceilings.

Content-modification tasks remain a substantial failure mode (as shown in the failure analysis), suggesting the method's benefits may be concentrated in navigation/information-seeking tasks rather than the harder, more valuable modification tasks.

strengths: The preliminary probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) is a sensible diagnostic framework that clearly motivates the need for grounding, and the large gap between short-horizon and long-horizon performance is a useful finding.

The paper provides extensive implementation details, prompts, and ablations in the appendix (cost-performance tradeoffs, adaptive branching/deduplication, listwise vs absolute reward, candidate size, cross-judge consistency), which aids reproducibility and shows thoroughness.

R-WoM is evaluated across multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5/3.7/4/4.5-Sonnet) and shows fairly consistent relative improvements over Vanilla, RAG, and WebDreamer baselines in both OSWorld and WebArena.
The extension to tutorial-scarce domains via self-play-based tutorial synthesis (Section 5.5) is a nice touch that partially addresses the method's core dependency on external tutorial availability.
Failure mode and retrieval-quality analyses (Tables 9-11, Figure 4) add useful qualitative insight into when and why the method helps or doesn't.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a curated subset of tasks explicitly selected for having available tutorials (87/361 OSWorld tasks, 113/301 WebArena templates), which directly biases the comparison in favor of a retrieval-augmented method; the paper does not report performance on the majority of tasks lacking tutorial coverage in the main experiments (only partially addressed via a small synthetic-tutorial extension on OSWorld in 5.5).

The probing analysis in Section 3 relies on very small sample sizes (100, 40, and 98 examples) spread across only three LLMs, which is a thin empirical basis for the paper's central claim that "LLMs fail at full-procedure planning" -- this is a widely intuitive and arguably unsurprising claim restated with limited new evidence.

The core technical contributions (query rewriting + LLM reranking RAG, LongCoT multi-step rollout instead of iterative rollout, listwise rather than absolute reward ranking) are each incremental combinations of existing, well-known techniques (DeepSeek-R1 style CoT, listwise ranking/LipO, standard RAG rerankers) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism for world modeling.

Absolute success rates remain quite low overall (roughly 25-40%), and the reported improvements, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms (e.g., Claude-3.5-Sonnet on WebArena: 30.70 to 33.15); some gains are within or close to the reported standard deviations across only three runs, raising questions about statistical robustness.

The oracle-tutorial experiment (Figure 4) shows that even with perfect retrieval, gains over grounded retrieval are often modest, suggesting the retrieval component itself is not the primary limiting factor and casting some doubt on how much the "grounding" story explains the improvements versus other confounds (e.g., additional inference-time compute/CoT length).

WebDreamer is reimplemented as a baseline rather than compared against its original reported numbers/setup, and no comparison is made against more recent iterative world-model baselines (e.g., WebEvolver, WKM) despite being discussed in related work, limiting the strength of the empirical positioning.

The paper does not discuss cost/latency trade-offs in the main text (only in the appendix), yet R-WoM's default version incurs substantially higher token costs (Table 8) than baselines, which should factor more prominently into the overall assessment of practical value.

strengths: Well-motivated systematic probing study decomposing LLM world-model capability into three concrete tasks (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition), providing clear empirical evidence for where LLMs fail (long-horizon procedural alignment) versus succeed (local transitions).

Comprehensive empirical validation across two realistic, challenging benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena) and three different backbone LLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet), with consistent relative improvements.

Extensive ablation studies covering retrieval quality (query rewriting + reranking), imagination horizon, oracle vs retrieved tutorial grounding, listwise vs absolute reward, candidate size, and cost-performance tradeoffs (adaptive branching/deduplication), which substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Practical engineering contributions (LongCoT single-pass rollout instead of iterative policy-world model communication, adaptive action branching, deduplication) that meaningfully reduce computational cost while retaining most performance gains, with concrete token/latency measurements.

Extension to tutorial-scarce settings via self-play trajectory synthesis (RQ4) broadens applicability and is tested on additional newer models (Claude-4/4.5-Sonnet), showing the method generalizes beyond the original three backbones.

Reasonable reproducibility: detailed prompts, action spaces, and pipeline algorithm are provided in the appendix, along with cross-judge consistency checks (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) to validate the LLM-judge-based evaluation.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: the core contribution largely combines existing ideas (RAG with query rewriting/reranking, listwise/relative reward modeling, LongCoT rollouts) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism for world modeling.

Evaluation subsets are small and selected based on tutorial availability (87/361 OSWorld tasks, 113/301 WebArena templates), which could bias results toward tasks where retrieval-based grounding is inherently more helpful, limiting claims of general applicability to the full benchmarks.

Probing task sample sizes are quite small (40 samples for full-procedure alignment, 98 for milestone recognition, 100 for next-state identification), raising concerns about statistical reliability of the preliminary analysis that motivates the whole paper.

The 'oracle'/reference tutorials and full-procedure alignment judgments are human-annotated by the authors, which could introduce subjective bias or leakage, especially since the same team also builds the R-WoM retrieval pipeline evaluated against these annotations.

Comparisons omit some directly relevant recent world-model baselines discussed in related work (e.g., WKM, WebEvolver), relying mainly on WebDreamer and plain RAG as baselines, which may understate the state of competition in grounded world modeling.

Error bars in Table 2 are occasionally large relative to the reported gains (e.g., Qwen OSWorld 26.36±2.32 vs 30.84±1.07), making some claimed improvements less statistically convincing without significance testing.
